segments.title: Why the Royal Navy needed a modern staff
segments.body: The counterfactual asks what follows if the Royal Navy receives a formal staff when the Army does. Its clearest consequences concern the preparations for World War I, since wartime events become harder to predict. Parts of a naval staff already existed, but their inherited organization fitted the political demands of the early twentieth century poorly. The Navy had modernized gradually throughout the nineteenth century, adding functions to existing offices. It could make an effective public case through the press and campaigns such as We Want Eight, while still expecting government ministers to accept its authority.

evidence.note: The patron's counterfactual, limits on predicting World War I, gradual naval staff reform, and the contrast between press campaigning and ministerial communication.

segments.summary: Gradual staff reform left the Royal Navy effective at public campaigning but poorly equipped to explain its strategy systematically to ministers.

segments.title: How the Esher Report made wartime failures usable
segments.body: The Esher Report illustrates the practical value of historical synthesis in government. Reports and testimony from different contributors need a common language and format before ministers can use them together. A historian can assemble that material without having written every underlying report. Here, the work connects the Boer War's logistical and organizational failures to the problems that Army reform needed to address.

evidence.note: Esher's report as an example of historians combining other people's evidence into a consistent, accessible account of wartime failures.

segments.summary: Historical synthesis helped turn separate accounts of Boer War failures into an accessible basis for Army reform.

segments.title: The Esher Report turns Boer War failure into Army reform
segments.body: The Boer War exposed operational, logistical, and organizational failures in the Army and War Office. The Esher Report recommended an Army Council modeled on the Board of Admiralty, a General Staff, and a Chief of the General Staff to replace the commander-in-chief of the forces. A stronger War Office would provide more civilian administrative support. Samuel Pepys illustrates the Navy's much older tradition of senior civil servants supporting naval administration. These recommendations borrowed from the Admiralty and adapted its practices to the Army's needs. In this comparison, reform let the Army move ahead of the Navy in formal staff organization during the first decade of the twentieth century.

evidence.note: Boer War lessons, the Esher recommendations, Samuel Pepys as a naval civil servant, and the Army's adoption and adaptation of Admiralty practice.

segments.summary: The Boer War inquiry translated operational, logistical, and organizational failures into a new Army Council, General Staff, and strengthened War Office.

segments.title: Haldane reforms and the Imperial General Staff
segments.body: Richard Haldane implemented the Esher proposals alongside reforms to the Territorial Army, expeditionary force, and Officer Training Corps. The Imperial General Staff brought officers from across the Empire together to develop common policy and compatible doctrine. Local forces could retain their character while becoming able to work together logistically. The Royal Navy already sent officers to advise developing Dominion navies, with strong results in Australia and more difficulty in Canada. In India, the British Army resisted naval investment that threatened its central position in imperial defence. A stronger War Office and Army Board supplied the staff needed to administer the force and brief political leaders regularly.

evidence.note: Haldane's implementation, common imperial doctrine and logistics, naval advisory work in Australia and Canada, and Army resistance to naval investment in India.

segments.summary: Haldane's reforms link the Territorial Army and expeditionary force to an Imperial General Staff designed to coordinate doctrine and logistics across the Empire.

segments.title: How Army briefings shaped ministers' defence priorities
segments.body: Haldane encouraged continuous Army briefings from 1905 to 1912, explaining capabilities, requirements, and concepts of operations. Ministers received papers they could study, while the Navy relied more on books, inherited influence, and conversations at social events. This resembles the way peacetime alliances, infrastructure, and language shape how allies and opponents approach a future conflict. Repeated Army briefings taught ministers to think first about the expeditionary force and imperial policing. The Navy's indispensable role in moving those forces and sustaining trade could then become an assumed supporting service. Systematic explanation gave the Army a way to challenge the Navy's much stronger inherited political position.

evidence.note: Army papers and briefings, Haldane's 1905-1912 role, peacetime shaping of assumptions, and the relegation of naval transport to an assumed supporting function.

segments.summary: Regular Army papers and briefings taught ministers to understand defence through an Army framework, while the Navy relied on inherited political influence.

segments.title: A General Staff still faced imperial distance and political obstacles
segments.body: The reformed Army had a General Staff to prepare papers and coordinate forces across the Empire. An Army Council supplied senior officers to direct and organize the service. Politicians and the distance between imperial forces still frustrated this work, so a formal organization did not remove every practical obstacle. Even with those limits, the assessment places the Army in a much stronger position than in the 1890s. Earlier wars had failed to force comparable institutional change.

evidence.note: General Staff coordination and Army Council leadership, constrained by politicians, distance, and geography despite major improvement over the 1890s.

segments.summary: Formal staff work improved Army coordination, though politicians and the geography of the Empire continued to obstruct it.

segments.title: Why technical corps dominated the new Army staff
segments.body: Royal Engineers and artillery officers were prominent in the reformed Army staff. Their branches already required examinations and mathematical training. These qualifications provided an available group of officers prepared for the new staff's work. The example links the composition of the staff to the professional education that its officers had received.

evidence.note: The Royal Engineers and artillery officers' examinations, mathematical training, and prominence in the new staff.

segments.summary: Royal Engineers and artillery officers supplied much of the reformed Army staff because their technical branches already selected and trained officers through examinations and mathematics.

segments.title: How the Admiralty divided work among the Sea Lords
segments.body: The Second Sea Lord oversaw personnel and manning, and generally held a higher naval rank than the Third Sea Lord. The Third Sea Lord's remit covered technology, construction, maintenance, and refit. Once a ship entered operational service, the Fourth Sea Lord organized its supplies around the world. Manning remained the Second Sea Lord's responsibility, while a ship returning for refit came back under the Third Sea Lord's remit. The First Sea Lord directed the fleet's employment but had little staff of his own beyond the Naval Intelligence Department.

evidence.note: Sea Lord rank and functional responsibilities, the transition between construction and operational supply, and the First Sea Lord's reliance on Naval Intelligence.

segments.summary: The Admiralty already divided personnel, construction and refit, logistics, and operational employment among senior Sea Lords.

segments.title: Naval Intelligence became a secretive shadow staff
segments.body: The Naval Intelligence Department began with foreign intelligence, then accumulated mobilization planning, war strategy, defence, and merchant-shipping protection. This gave the Royal Navy a de facto staff inside an intelligence organization. Protecting sources and concealing plans encouraged intelligence officers to withhold information, including the fact that they possessed it. The Second, Third, and Fourth Sea Lords could explain personnel, construction, and supply requirements to the press or Parliament. Naval strategy sat in an office reluctant to communicate in the same way. The criticism concerns where staff work was placed and how it reached government, rather than the absence of planning.

evidence.note: Naval Intelligence's accumulation of mobilization, war strategy, defence, and trade protection, and secrecy as an obstacle to communicating naval plans.

segments.summary: Mobilization, strategy, defence, and trade-protection functions accumulated inside Naval Intelligence, creating capable planning machinery that resisted sharing information.

segments.title: From Naval Intelligence to an Admiralty War Staff
segments.body: A reform of the whole organization would have separated intelligence from the other staff functions accumulating around it. Each function needed a clear place under the Sea Lords and a route to the Board of Admiralty. The comparison looks forward to the development of the Admiralty War Staff and its further evolution during World War I. Prince Louis of Battenberg already supervised intelligence, mobilization, strategy, defence, and trade protection, receiving credit here for extensive war preparation often associated with Fisher. His competence did not resolve the problem of communicating work held inside an intelligence department. Internal reform proceeded slowly because existing arrangements still worked well enough for the Navy to retain them.

evidence.note: The proposed separation of intelligence from general staff functions, wartime staff evolution, Battenberg's planning responsibilities, and the department's internal focus.

segments.summary: The proposed 1905 reform anticipates the wartime separation of intelligence from operations, strategy, mobilization, and broader staff work.

segments.title: Why Lloyd George could reform the Admiralty
segments.body: The scenario needs a cabinet minister able to challenge the Admiralty without adopting its views automatically. Churchill is excluded at this starting point because he is outside the cabinet, while David Lloyd George holds the Board of Trade. Lloyd George preferred peace and lower defence expenditure, and was lukewarm about empire, but wanted to reform the institutions available to him. He would demand explanations of naval policy and spending. His later insistence as prime minister on weekly naval papers supplies the historical example: recent operations and plans for the next week had to connect to an explicit strategy.

evidence.note: External reform through a cabinet minister, Lloyd George's Board of Trade position, preference for lower spending, and later insistence on weekly naval briefings.

segments.summary: David Lloyd George's cabinet position and reforming approach make him the proposed First Lord for a naval reorganization in 1905.

segments.title: Four strategic goals make naval policy legible to cabinet
segments.body: The wartime naval appreciation quoted from Andrew Boyd's work on British naval intelligence opened with four strategic goals. These were protecting sea communications for British and Allied armies, especially in France, eliminating enemy trade to weaken military capacity and the will to fight, protecting Allied commerce, and preventing invasion or raids on the United Kingdom. The goals gave cabinet a concise framework for interpreting naval operations. Lloyd George's preference for recurring departmental explanations supplies a model for monthly papers in peacetime. Appointing him First Lord with a reforming mandate in 1905 would bring that practice into the Admiralty earlier.

evidence.note: Four strategic goals in the wartime naval appreciation quoted from Andrew Boyd, and their use as a model for monthly departmental explanations in the counterfactual.

segments.summary: Lloyd George's wartime naval appreciation defined two offensive and two defensive goals, providing a model for concise monthly Admiralty papers in peacetime.

segments.title: A counterfactual Admiralty Board for 1905
segments.body: The counterfactual largely retains the Second and Third Sea Lords' existing departments. It adds a third political representative, an additional civil lord, to strengthen the Navy's position in the House of Commons and its communication with ministers. The First Lord remains president of the board, while the First Sea Lord gains a general staff responsible for strategy, defence, and mobilization. The civil lord's responsibilities for civilian holdings fit alongside the Second Sea Lord's work. An additional civil lord oversees contracts and commitments beside the Third Sea Lord's technology, construction, maintenance, and refit responsibilities.

evidence.note: Three political representatives and the proposed pairing of civil lords with Sea Lords, plus strategy, defence, and mobilization under the First Sea Lord.

segments.summary: The proposed board gives the First Sea Lord a coordinating staff and pairs naval officers with ministers responsible for explaining and overseeing their work.

segments.title: Why trade protection belongs beside naval logistics
segments.body: The proposed Fourth Sea Lord combines logistics with trade protection. Planning merchant protection and organizing the movement of supplies require closely related work. The wartime convoy system supplies the comparison, with officers from the Fourth Sea Lord's organization helping to run it. Placing these functions together in 1905 would give them a common administrative home before the war.

evidence.note: Proposed combination of logistics and trade protection, supported by the Fourth Sea Lord's staff contribution to wartime convoy organization.

segments.summary: The proposed reorganization joins supply and trade protection under the Fourth Sea Lord, drawing on their later connection in convoy administration.

segments.title: A Fifth Sea Lord separates secret intelligence from public explanations
segments.body: A new Fifth Sea Lord would give intelligence its own representative at the board. Intelligence estimates would go to cabinet members and the Committee of Imperial Defence as appropriate. Other departments could circulate monthly accounts of their work, with fuller papers for ministers and reduced versions for Parliament. Political ministers would supply covering explanations. Most of the staff already existed, so the proposal redistributes Naval Intelligence's accumulated functions and probably promotes Battenberg to the new post. Giving the First Sea Lord direct responsibility for strategy and mobilization would also require that office to produce and discuss its plans.

evidence.note: A proposed intelligence Sea Lord, restricted circulation of estimates, monthly political briefings, redistribution of existing staff, and Battenberg as a possible appointee.

segments.summary: A dedicated intelligence Sea Lord could preserve restricted estimates while the wider Admiralty explained its work regularly to cabinet and Parliament.

segments.title: Fisher and Lloyd George collide over naval reform
segments.body: The scenario places an imperial-minded First Sea Lord beside a minister less committed to empire and determined to control defence spending. Fisher would initially resist reform, then recognize the new staff as a means of influencing government policy more effectively. Lloyd George would still want Britain to retain its international position. His scrutiny would focus on whether fleet reductions weakened presence and interrupted the flow of trade. That interest in what Britain could do with control of the sea suggests a productive relationship with Julian Corbett after initial disagreements. HMS Dreadnought would still be built as she was, while subsequent orders would face different questions about their purpose.

evidence.note: Fisher's initial resistance and incentive to communicate, Lloyd George's trade priorities, Dreadnought's unchanged construction, and possible agreement with Corbett.

segments.summary: Fisher could embrace the new staff as a route to influence, while Lloyd George would test naval spending against trade, presence, and economic security.

segments.title: Trade and economic growth give naval strength a different purpose
segments.body: More cruisers are the expected procurement change, while battleship construction remains tied to the quantitative competition with Germany. Lloyd George's interest in technology leaves room for faster development of ship armament as well. Infrastructure and national strength serve his desire for enough stability to keep trade flowing. In this account of his priorities, commerce and economic growth support efforts to reduce poverty and improve living conditions. The resulting case for naval power connects fleet spending to the conditions needed for a trading economy.

evidence.note: More cruisers, continued German influence on battleship numbers, technical and infrastructure interests, and trade-led growth as Lloyd George's rationale for peace through strength.

segments.summary: Lloyd George's priorities connect naval strength with stable trade and economic growth, suggesting more cruisers while battleship numbers remain tied to Germany.

segments.title: GDP per person and total economic capacity answer different questions
segments.body: GDP per capita is treated as a useful quick guide with limits as a measure of national economic strength. The Britain-Mississippi comparison illustrates the problem: higher output per person does not establish which economy is larger in total. Population and the scale of the whole economy remain relevant to that second question. A per-person figure therefore needs context before it becomes an argument about a state's overall economic capacity.

evidence.note: The Britain-Mississippi illustration distinguishes GDP per capita from total economic scale. Numerical estimates and the hypothetical world ranking are not independently established here.

segments.summary: A Britain-Mississippi comparison distinguishes output per person from the total resources represented by an economy.

segments.title: Trade economics reshape imperial naval coordination
segments.body: The economic priorities in this prewar argument are the balance of trade and the flow of materials. Britain still depends on industry, with raw materials arriving by sea and manufactured goods moving outward. Lloyd George's interest in those flows could make coordination with Dominion navies part of his Admiralty reforms. A general staff would help persuade them to buy ships and equipment, supplying orders for British industry while expanding imperial naval capacity. The counterfactual carries the priorities he pursued at the Board of Trade into the department responsible for naval policy, supported by a reforming mandate.

evidence.note: Prewar trade and industrial priorities, Dominion purchases of ships and equipment, and the transfer of Lloyd George's Board of Trade arguments into the counterfactual Admiralty.

segments.summary: Lloyd George's focus on trade flows and industrial strength could make imperial naval coordination an economic policy as well as a defence policy.

segments.title: Trade protection expands the battlecruiser program
segments.body: Fisher could present battlecruisers to Lloyd George as instruments of economic warfare and global trade protection. The battle fleet gains control of the ocean, while fast capital cruisers exercise that control and keep commerce moving. A minister convinced by that argument would press for more ships. The possible program expands the Lion, Queen Mary, and Tiger groups, with two or even three of the later designs considered. Annual orders might settle at four or five battleships and a couple of battlecruisers, depending on German construction. Rising costs could also revive interest in 9.2-inch-gunned cruisers. These are alternative possibilities, and the largest battlecruiser orders would take resources from battleship construction.

evidence.note: Battlecruisers as tools of economic warfare, possible class and annual order totals, cheaper 9.2-inch cruisers, and pressure on battleship construction in the largest program.

segments.summary: Fisher's battlecruisers become attractive as instruments for exercising sea control and protecting global commerce, potentially increasing annual orders.

segments.title: Dominion battlecruisers share imperial defence costs
segments.body: Australia and New Zealand supply precedents for asking other parts of the Empire to support capital cruisers. Canada and India could also receive ships, while trade-protection needs might justify more than one for Canada or Australia. Transferring older ships at reduced cost would let Dominion governments assume their running expenses while Britain retained access to their capability. One version builds thirteen ships, with four operated in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and India and nine remaining under British operation. Another allocation distributes all three Invincibles overseas, including one for a New Zealand navy established earlier than in actual history. The precise totals and Tiger completion dates remain open. The proposal increases total spending, but shifts some long-term costs away from Britain's naval estimate.

evidence.note: Dominion ownership and transfer options, variable thirteen-ship arithmetic, overseas Invincibles, and the distinction between total costs and Britain's share.

segments.summary: Older battlecruisers could pass to Dominion navies, preserving imperial access to the ships while shifting operating costs away from Britain's naval budget.

segments.title: Why Dominion battlecruisers suited Britain's imperial position
segments.body: South Africa is another possible participant in the counterfactual naval program. Its growing involvement in imperial Army projects suggests a parallel route into naval cooperation. Battlecruisers fit Britain's trade-protection requirements better than Dominion battleships in this argument. Keeping the stronger battleship force would also leave Britain able to impose its will on a battlecruiser force if necessary. The proposed distribution therefore combines overseas defence with continued British naval superiority.

evidence.note: South Africa as a possible naval participant, the trade-protection rationale for Dominion battlecruisers, and Britain's ability to enforce its will through a superior battleship force.

segments.summary: Dominion battlecruisers could protect imperial trade while Britain's battleships retained the power to enforce its will if required.

segments.title: Global reactions to an imperial battlecruiser network
segments.body: A larger British battlecruiser program would put pressure on Germany's procurement without, in this assessment, straining Britain's shipbuilding infrastructure. France and Italy would probably change little, while Japan and the United States would have to take account of more imperial capital ships in the Pacific. A Canadian ship on the Pacific coast, alongside ships operating from India and Australia, would make that presence especially visible. The argument distinguishes the German construction figures used to justify British battleship numbers from the worldwide commerce used to justify battlecruisers. Lloyd George could support the latter as protection for trade while asking the Dominions to carry more of the cost.

evidence.note: Projected foreign responses and British construction capacity, Pacific deployments, and the different political justifications for battleships and battlecruisers.

segments.summary: An expanded British and Dominion battlecruiser force pressures Germany and draws Japanese and American attention to a heavier imperial presence in the Pacific.

segments.title: A post-1908 capital-ship building standard
segments.body: Experience at the Admiralty could leave Chancellor Lloyd George more familiar with the Navy's case, even while opposing reckless spending. A regular capital-ship formula might avert the We Want Eight campaign. The preferred version here is five battleships and one battlecruiser per order, with 15-inch-gunned Tiger derivatives accompanying the Queen Elizabeth and Revenge classes. The projected force would have two Tigers and two 15-inch-gunned Tiger derivatives, compared here with the historical Renown and Repulse. Another possibility is four battleships and two battlecruisers, so the construction formula is not fixed. Trade-protection priorities would also favor destroyers and anti-submarine work within the limited capabilities of the period.

evidence.note: Lloyd George's hypothetical move to the Treasury, alternative regular orders, improved Tigers with 15-inch guns, Renown and Repulse, destroyers, and limited early anti-submarine work.

segments.summary: Prior experience at the Admiralty could lead Chancellor Lloyd George to accept a steady annual mix of battleships and battlecruisers without the We Want Eight crisis.

segments.title: Briefings mobilize Dominion naval resources
segments.body: A wider imperial fleet depends on Dominion governments understanding the roles and costs they would assume. Regular briefings could encourage naval investment in the same way that Army briefings supported the growth of imperial land forces. This would take time and would not win votes or arguments immediately. Repeated explanations could nevertheless establish the language in which supporters and opponents debated naval policy. The projected result is more ships across the Empire without a comparable increase in Britain's own naval spending.

evidence.note: Regular Dominion briefings as a gradual means of encouraging naval expenditure and shaping debate, with no claim of immediate political success.

segments.summary: Regular imperial briefings could persuade Dominion governments to fund naval growth and argue within a strategic framework set by the Admiralty.

segments.title: Two meanings of 'battlecruiser' in this scenario
segments.body: The terminology here uses spacing to distinguish two related ship concepts. 'Battle cruiser' in two words denotes the armoured-cruiser lineage, while the one-word form refers to ships designed more directly for fighting. The latter have greater subdivision and armour coverage, though still less complete protection than a fast battleship. This distinction accompanies a projected total of up to fourteen ships across the two categories. Seven carry 13.5-inch guns, with two 15-inch-gunned ships expected to enter service soon afterward. These are the working totals for the counterfactual, whose earlier class-by-class options vary.

evidence.note: The local distinction between battle cruiser and battlecruiser, subdivision and armour limits, and a projected fleet of up to fourteen with seven 13.5-inch ships and two 15-inch ships to follow.

segments.summary: Here, the two-word 'battle cruiser' denotes the armoured-cruiser lineage, while 'battlecruiser' denotes a more heavily protected fighting ship.

segments.title: A unified Army-Navy war plan against Germany
segments.body: Sir George Clarke's historical effort to create a unified plan lacked enough political backing: Haldane supported him, but the prime minister did not act. In the counterfactual, Haldane and Lloyd George can press together for coordinated Army and Navy assumptions. Their case also appeals to Lloyd George's concern with efficient spending. The British Expeditionary Force would probably still go to France, within a more coordinated approach to war with Germany.

evidence.note: Sir George Clarke's unsuccessful unified planning effort, Haldane's support, possible additional support from Lloyd George, and the continued expectation of a BEF deployment to France. The spoken date sequence is unclear.

segments.summary: A stronger naval staff gives the Committee of Imperial Defence a better chance to reconcile Army and Navy plans before war with Germany.

segments.title: A Dominion expeditionary force for maritime strategy
segments.body: The proposed compromise groups Canadian, Australian, New Zealand, South African, Indian, Royal Marine, and possibly British Army formations into an imperial expeditionary force. One outline uses three corps of three divisions, with the composition left open. Alex Clarke recalls encountering a similar notion in a period paper, but gives no bibliographic reference and says it attracted no support. A reorganized Fourth Sea Lord's office could supply transport and shipping taken up from trade to land the force in another theatre. It could attack German colonies while the main British Expeditionary Force served in France, supported and expanded by the Territorials. The Navy would still hold the North Sea. In the counterfactual, coordinated staff work makes these commitments compatible without a fundamentally different budget.

evidence.note: The hypothetical imperial force, an unreferenced personal recollection of a period proposal, transport through the Fourth Sea Lord, colonial operations, and the Army-Navy compromise.

segments.summary: The British Expeditionary Force still goes to France, while a Dominion formation and naval transport capacity open secondary theatres and attack German colonies.

segments.title: Dogger Bank with more British battlecruisers
segments.body: The larger force would make 12-inch-gunned ships less likely to be needed at Dogger Bank. Seven 13.5-inch ships would be available in the projected fleet, leaving five even if two were absent. A 15-inch-gunned battlecruiser might join them if construction had begun alongside the Queen Elizabeths. With their fire-control system as well, it would offer a possible new flagship for Beatty. He might still make the same mistakes, and the outcome remains uncertain, but the available firepower and accompanying cruiser force would differ substantially.

evidence.note: Possible Dogger Bank availability of five 13.5-inch ships and a 15-inch battlecruiser, depending on absences and construction timing.
Beatty's possible flagship, Queen Elizabeth-style fire control, additional cruisers, and the possibility that the same command errors persist.

segments.summary: Extra heavy-gunned battlecruisers could change Dogger Bank's firepower even if Beatty repeated his command errors.

segments.title: The German Army's budget limits the response to extra British ships
segments.body: Germany would have to spend more to answer the larger British battlecruiser force. In this interpretation, the Army tolerates naval expansion until it encroaches on its own budget. The Kaiser's support for naval growth does not remove that institutional constraint. Additional British construction could therefore bring the quantitative race to an earlier end by making the competing German claims on money harder to reconcile.

evidence.note: Extra German naval spending as a response to Britain, Army resistance to losing its budget, and an earlier end to the quantitative naval race as a possible result.

segments.summary: Matching a larger British battlecruiser force could bring German naval spending into conflict with the Army's budget earlier.

segments.title: How distributed battlecruisers could constrain German wartime movements
segments.body: A Canadian Invincible-class ship could threaten von Spee's East Asia Squadron from the eastern Pacific. One projected movement takes it toward Panama and then south, while other imperial battlecruisers cover Asian waters. Von Spee might still choose his historical route, but the opposing forces could close it more quickly. Extra capital ships in the Mediterranean would also affect German movements there. Their positions and actions are too uncertain to predict the resulting course of World War I. The firmer expectation within the scenario is a larger Royal Navy and better prepared British strategy.

evidence.note: A Canadian Invincible's possible movement toward Panama and south, von Spee's narrowing options, additional Mediterranean ships, and limits on predicting wartime events. The Mediterranean ship name is unclear.

segments.summary: A Canadian Invincible and other imperial capital cruisers would narrow von Spee's options, though the resulting wartime movements remain unpredictable.

segments.title: Dominion sea power changes the postwar treaty problem
segments.body: The closing counterfactual assumes that World War I ends broadly as it did historically. It allows a changed Dogger Bank to damage the German scouting force so badly that a later Jutland-style operation does not occur. Several Dominion governments would by then have spent nearly a decade learning the value of sea power and operating their own capital cruisers. Australia would consequently be one of several imperial naval powers whose interests Britain had to accommodate. The expectation is that some Washington Naval Treaty agreements would fail under those conditions. The precise settlement remains an open question for viewers.

evidence.note: An open postwar counterfactual about experienced Dominion capital-ship powers and Washington treaty agreements, conditional on broadly similar wartime outcomes.

segments.summary: A decade of Dominion naval investment would make the Washington Naval Treaty settlement harder to reproduce after World War I.
